superficial

/soo-per-FISH-uhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Superficial means existing or occurring only on the surface; lacking real depth or substance.

The doctor reassured the family that the cut was only superficial, needing nothing more than a bandage.

Example

The consultant's forty-page report on the company's problems turned out to be a superficial skim of publicly available news articles, offering no new data and no insight the executives couldn't have found themselves in an afternoon of searching online.

The report only appeared thorough; it never actually dug beneath the surface of well-known information, which is exactly what "superficial" describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

skin-deep: Skin-deep is the vivid, informal cousin of superficial: it stays literally at the surface — skin-deep beauty, a skin-deep wound. Superficial ranges wider and sounds more formal, covering analyses, relationships, and understandings that lack real depth.

hasty: Hasty faults speed: something done in too much of a hurry — a hasty exit, a hasty decision. Superficial faults depth: the work never gets beneath the surface, however long it took. A report can be slow, polished, and still superficial.

token: Token describes a bare-minimum gesture made so an obligation looks met — a token effort, a token apology. Superficial measures depth, not sincerity of the gesture: a superficial study may be earnest and full-length yet still never dig beneath the surface.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

thorough: complete and careful, examining every important detail

profound: showing or involving genuine depth of thought or understanding

Where it sits · how little depth it reaches

cursory → shallow → superficial

cursory vs. superficial: A cursory glance takes in only the first, most obvious details — milder than superficial, because a quick look can be followed by a deeper one, while something superficial never leaves the surface at all.

shallow vs. superficial: A shallow analysis covers the topic without ever digging beneath its surface — and superficial goes a step further, staying so completely on the surface that no real substance is touched at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — super-: above, over

Root — fici-: face, surface, form (Latin facies)

Suffix — -al: relating to

Put it together: "superficial" literally means "relating to what's above/on the surface" — the faci- root, meaning "face" or "surface," combined with super- ("over") describes anything that stays on top, never reaching what lies beneath.

Use the root in a new word: facade: Behind the elegant facade of the old bank building, the interior had long since crumbled into disrepair.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral to critical

Superficial is usually mildly critical — describing an analysis, wound, or relationship as superficial suggests it lacks the depth it perhaps should have. It can be literal (a superficial scratch) or figurative (a superficial understanding of a topic).
